case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a notice of appeal filed after a district court has announced a decision but before entry of a final judgment can be treated as effective once final judgment is later entered (i.e., under the cumulative-finality doctrine or a related rule).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (final-decision rule) and Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4 (timing/effectiveness of notices of appeal, including the premature-notice framework).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Parrish argues that his notice of appeal should be deemed valid despite being filed before the case was technically final because, under the long-recognized cumulative-finality doctrine (and related premature-notice principles), the later entry of a final judgment cures the prematurity; he emphasizes that rejecting the appeal on timing formalities undermines fair access to appellate review, especially for incarcerated litigants facing substantial legal-mail delays.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States’ position (as reflected across the filings you provided) is that the court should apply a rule that preserves appellate jurisdiction in this posture—either because cumulative finality (or an equivalent premature-notice rule) makes the notice effective once final judgment is entered, or because the timing defect should not defeat jurisdiction when finality is achieved before the appeal is adjudicated; the government therefore supports a resolution that validates the appeal rather than dismissing it on technical timing grounds.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Rule 4(a)(2) should not be read to “cure” prematurity in a way that loosens § 1291’s finality constraint, but that objection loses force because the Rule’s own text makes the notice effective only “on the date of and after” entry—so no jurisdiction vests until final judgment exists. Justice Barrett’s administrable limit, drawn from FirsTier, is the narrow ground I would adopt: relation-forward applies only when the announced decision would be appealable if immediately reduced to judgment, which prevents parties from laundering interlocutory appeals. Justice Thomas’s textual point reinforces that this is not an equitable expansion of jurisdiction but a rule-based timing mechanism authorized by the Rules Enabling Act and already cabined by precedent. On a minimalist approach, we can resolve this case by applying FirsTier’s limiting construction and reserving edge cases involving nonfinal announced rulings or prejudice.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest contrary point—Justice Sotomayor’s earlier worry that we would be "creating" appellate jurisdiction—fails on the enacted text of Rule 4(a)(2), which makes a premature notice effective only "on the date of and after" entry of judgment, so § 1291 finality remains the jurisdictional trigger. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett correctly rely on FirsTier’s limiting construction: relation-forward applies only when the announced disposition would be appealable if immediately reduced to judgment, preventing any laundering of interlocutory orders into appealable ones. Under a strict textualist approach, that is not an equitable enlargement of jurisdiction but a timing rule authorized by the Rules Enabling Act and consistent with Article III because jurisdiction attaches only after final judgment exists. No colleague has identified any precedent or statutory text that requires reading Rule 4(a)(2) more narrowly in this final-in-all-but-entry posture.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that we should avoid forfeiture from a premature notice and not let clerical timing defeat access to review, particularly for incarcerated litigants. But under my methodology the controlling answer is textual: as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, Rule 4(a)(2) expressly treats a notice filed after an announced dispositive decision and before entry as filed “on the date of and after the entry,” so no jurisdiction vests until § 1291 finality actually exists. FirsTier matters because it supplies the limiting construction that defeats the petitioner-side worry about expanding jurisdiction: relation-forward applies only when the announced decision would be appealable if immediately entered as judgment, which keeps this from becoming a free-floating cumulative-finality doctrine. Because that boundary is rule-based and administrable, dismissing here would create a needless trap without any corresponding protection of finality.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest opposing argument remains that treating a premature notice as effective would “manufacture” appellate jurisdiction and erode § 1291’s finality rule. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Rule 4(a)(2)’s text makes the notice effective only “on the date of and after” entry of judgment, so jurisdiction still does not vest until a final, appealable judgment exists; that answers the Article III/§ 1291 worry rather than evading it. Barrett’s reliance on FirsTier supplies the crucial limiting principle—relation-forward only when the announced disposition would be appealable if immediately reduced to judgment—preventing any laundering of interlocutory orders into appeals. On my pragmatic, access-to-justice view, that narrow, administrable rule avoids a forfeiture trap (often borne by pro se and incarcerated litigants) without expanding final-judgment jurisdiction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The best opposing point was the jurisdictional concern (initially pressed by Justice Sotomayor) that validating an early notice would "create" appellate jurisdiction and dilute § 1291 finality, but Rule 4(a)(2)’s text answers that by making the notice effective only "on the date of and after" entry—so jurisdiction still attaches only once a final judgment exists. As Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice emphasize, FirsTier supplies the necessary limiting construction: relation-forward applies only when the announced disposition would be appealable if immediately reduced to judgment, preventing interlocutory laundering and preserving statutory coherence. On a pragmatic textualist view, dismissing here would impose a pointless timing trap tied to ministerial entry without serving finality or reliance interests. No colleague has identified a precedent that narrows Rule 4(a)(2) beyond FirsTier on these facts, so my position is reinforced, not undermined.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that we must not let Rule 4(a)(2) become an equitable device that effectively loosens § 1291’s final-judgment rule, especially for incarcerated litigants. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the Rule’s text makes the notice effective only “on the date of and after the entry” of judgment, and FirsTier cabins that relation-forward mechanism to cases where the announced disposition would be appealable if immediately entered—so no appellate jurisdiction vests until finality actually exists. That limiting construction answers the slippery-slope concern about interlocutory orders while still avoiding the jurisdictional forfeiture that fairness concerns highlight. Because this approach applies the enacted Rule and our precedent without enlarging § 1291, I see no legal basis to change my vote.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that we must not erode § 1291’s final-judgment rule by allowing jurisdiction to arise from “prematurity,” but Rule 4(a)(2) as construed in FirsTier answers that: the notice does not confer appellate jurisdiction until final judgment is actually entered, so finality remains the jurisdictional hinge. Chief Justice Roberts’s limiting principle—that relation-forward applies only when the announced decision would be appealable if immediately entered and where no prejudice is shown—provides the administrable boundary that prevents this from morphing into a general cumulative-finality doctrine. Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas reinforce, in my view correctly, that this is not an equitable exception but an application of the Rules’ text adopted under the Rules Enabling Act, consistent with history, precedent, and institutional legitimacy. Because the approach avoids a needless trap without expanding § 1291 merits jurisdiction, I remain with the Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest objection—initially pressed by Justice Sotomayor—is that treating a premature notice as effective would erode § 1291’s final-judgment rule by “manufacturing” jurisdiction. But the text of Rule 4(a)(2) answers that concern by making the notice effective only “on the date of and after” entry of judgment, so jurisdiction still attaches only when finality actually exists. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on FirsTier provides the necessary limiting construction—relation-forward applies only when the announced disposition would be appealable if immediately reduced to judgment—preventing parties from laundering interlocutory orders into appellate jurisdiction. No colleague has identified any conflicting precedent or textual hook that would justify narrowing Rule 4(a)(2) further in this final-in-all-but-entry posture.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The best opposing argument—pressed earlier by Justice Sotomayor—is that we should not “create” appellate jurisdiction by crediting a notice filed before final judgment, because that risks eroding § 1291 and harming procedural regularity. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively answer that Rule 4(a)(2) does not vest jurisdiction early; by its text it merely makes the notice effective only “on the date of and after” the later entry of a judgment, and FirsTier’s limiting construction (only when the announced disposition would be appealable if immediately entered) supplies an administrable boundary against laundering interlocutory appeals. On my pragmatic, fairness-centered view, that approach avoids a timing trap—especially for pro se and incarcerated litigants—without stretching jurisdictional doctrine, and no colleague has identified prejudice or a nonfinal “announced decision” feature that would take this case outside FirsTier. Accordingly, I remain with the Respondent under the narrow, rule- and precedent-bound rationale Roberts/Barrett articulate.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-decision requirement is satisfied once final judgment is entered, and Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(2) reflects a settled practice that a notice filed after the court announces its dispositive decision but before entry of judgment is treated as filed on the date of entry. Under FirsTier Mortgage Co. v. Investors Mortgage Ins. Co., 498 U.S. 269 (1991), a premature notice can “ripen” when the later ministerial act of entering final judgment occurs, avoiding dismissal on a timing technicality without expanding appellate jurisdiction beyond finality. A narrow ruling validating the notice here promotes institutional legitimacy and uniform administration of Rule 4 while respecting the final-judgment rule because the appeal proceeds only after final judgment exists. To the extent there is uncertainty at the margins, the appropriate course is to apply Rule 4(a)(2)’s principle (or cumulative finality as a background rule) only where the earlier decision would have been appealable upon entry and no party is prejudiced.

Investors Mortgage Insurance Co., 498 U.S. 269 (1991), construed Rule 4(a)(2) to codify the longstanding practice of allowing such premature notices to relate forward, thereby preserving appellate jurisdiction once judgment is entered. Applying that rule here respects the enacted procedural text rather than judicially created traps and does not expand Article III jurisdiction beyond a final judgment because the notice becomes effective only upon final entry. Accordingly, the premature notice should be treated as effective when final judgment later issues.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I would treat Parrish’s notice of appeal as effective once final judgment was entered because Rule 4(a)(2) expressly provides that a notice filed after the court announces a decision but before entry of judgment is treated as filed on the date of and after entry, and this Court approved that relation-forward principle under the final-decision framework of 28 U.S.C. § 1291. In FirsTier Mortgage Co. v. Investors Mortgage Insurance Co., we recognized that Rule 4(a)(2) codifies a longstanding, practical approach that avoids forfeiting appellate review over technical timing defects when the case becomes final before the appeal is heard. Given the access-to-justice concerns at stake—especially for incarcerated litigants facing mail delays—dismissing for prematurity would elevate form over fairness without serving any legitimate jurisdictional purpose once finality has occurred. The better reading is that cumulative finality (or its Rule 4 analogue) cures the prematurity and preserves appellate jurisdiction.

Investors Mortgage Ins. Co., 498 U.S. 269 (1991), confirms that this “relate-forward” principle codifies a longstanding practice that promotes workable, non-technical administration of appellate jurisdiction. Where finality exists by the time the court of appeals acts, validating the notice avoids pointless duplicate filings, advances statutory coherence with § 1291, and better serves fair access to review without undermining any party’s reliance interests. The cumulative-finality/premature-notice doctrine is thus the sound, administrable middle ground: it enforces finality while preventing forfeiture based on timing formalities.

case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (final-decision rule) and Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4 (timing/effectiveness of a notice of appeal), as applied in the context of post-conviction proceedings (typically under 28 U.S.C. § 2255).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Parrish argues that his premature notice of appeal should be treated as effective once the district court ultimately entered a final judgment (or otherwise fully disposed of the case), relying on the long-recognized cumulative-finality doctrine to avoid forfeiture of appellate review based on a technical timing trap—especially where the timing problems are exacerbated by prison mail delays beyond an inmate’s control.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States’ position across the filings is that the Fourth Circuit’s dismissal rested on the absence of a final, appealable decision at the time of the notice and that the notice was not one that the rules or doctrine properly treat as ripening upon later finality; however, on the merits after certiorari, the government supports petitioner, indicating agreement that the notice should be deemed valid under the correct understanding of cumulative finality/Rule 4 principles (and that the Fourth Circuit applied an unduly rigid approach).

Justice Kavanaugh’s Microsoft v. Baker warning is important, yet it cuts differently here because final judgment is entered in the ordinary course rather than manufactured by the parties, so the appeal still rests on a true final decision. I would keep the holding narrow and administrable—limited to notices filed after an announced disposition that would be appealable upon entry and followed by an actual final judgment disposing of all claims—so we respect § 1291 while maintaining institutional legitimacy.
